title: Git & Version Control
summary: Git is a tiny content-addressed database of snapshots, and branches are just sticky notes pointing at one of those snapshots. Everything else is convenience on top.

blocks.markdown:
Git stores **snapshots**, not diffs — every commit captures the whole tree (deduplicated, so it's cheap).

- Everything is an **object** named by a hash of its content: **blobs**, **trees**, **commits**.
- A **branch** is just a file holding one commit hash. Creating one is free and instant.
- **Merge** keeps history and adds a commit; **rebase** rewrites commits onto a new base.
- **Golden rule:** never rewrite history others have already pulled.

blocks.subTitle: Which command
blocks.markdown:
Pick the tool for the job.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Integrate a finished branch, keep history | `git merge` |
| Clean up your own local commits | `git rebase -i` |
| Update branch with latest main, linear | `git rebase main` |
| Find which commit broke a test | `git bisect` |
| Already-pushed shared branch | merge, never rebase |

blocks.subTitle: The object model
blocks.markdown:
Once the object database clicks, the rest is obvious.

![Git object model: commit to tree to blobs](assets/git-version-control/object-model.svg)

- **Blob** — raw file bytes, named by content hash. The filename is *not* stored; identical files share one blob.
- **Tree** — a directory listing: name → mode → hash (blob or subtree).
- **Commit** — points to one top-level tree, its parent(s), author, and message.

A commit's hash includes its parent's, so the chain is tamper-evident.

assets.alt: Git object model: commit to tree to blobs

blocks.subTitle: Refs & HEAD
blocks.markdown:
A branch is just a pointer — which is why branching is O(1).

- A **branch** is a file under `.git/refs/heads/` holding one commit hash.
- **HEAD** points to the branch you're currently on.
- Committing creates the new object, then moves the current branch's ref forward — writing ~41 bytes.
- **Detached HEAD** = HEAD points straight at a commit, not a branch; new commits there are easily lost.

blocks.subTitle: The staging area
blocks.markdown:
The **index** (staging area) sits between your files and the repository, listing what the *next* commit will contain.

- **Working directory** — your actual files on disk.
- **Index** — the proposed next snapshot. `git add` copies a file's current content in.
- **Repository** — `git commit` turns the index into a permanent commit.

This lets you craft commits precisely — stage some files, or even part of one with `git add -p`.

blocks.subTitle: Merge vs rebase
blocks.markdown:
Integrating work means reconciling two pointers that diverged from a common ancestor.

![Merge keeps both lines; rebase replays onto main](assets/git-version-control/merge-vs-rebase.svg)

- **Merge** — creates a commit with *two* parents, preserving the parallel history.
- **Rebase** — replays your commits onto a new base as **brand-new commits** (new hashes); the originals are abandoned.
- **Fast-forward** — if main hasn't moved, Git just slides the pointer; no merge commit.

assets.alt: Merge keeps both lines; rebase replays onto main

blocks.subTitle: Conflicts
blocks.markdown:
Git merges at the line level with a **three-way merge** — your version, theirs, and the common **merge base**.

- A region changed on only one side → Git takes it automatically.
- A **conflict** arises only when the *same lines* changed on both sides.
- Git writes both versions between `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` markers and waits.
- You edit to resolve, then `git add` the file and continue.

blocks.subTitle: A feature flow
blocks.markdown:
Watch the objects and pointers move through a real feature.

```bash
git switch -c add-limit    # new ref -> current commit, move HEAD
git add limiter.js         # file bytes -> blob, into index
git commit -m "Add limiter" # build tree + commit, ref moves
git rebase -i main         # squash local noise (unpushed only!)
git push -u origin add-limit  # then open a pull request
```

The local part is milliseconds of tiny file writes — the expensive part is human review.

blocks.subTitle: Finding a bad commit
blocks.markdown:
**`git bisect`** binary-searches history to find the commit that introduced a bug.

- Mark a known-**good** and known-**bad** commit; Git checks out the midpoint.
- You test and say good/bad; it halves the range each step.
- That's **O(log n)** — about 9 tests for 500 commits, not 500.
- Automate it: `git bisect run <test-script>`.

blocks.subTitle: Merge vs rebase, decided
blocks.markdown:
The merge-vs-rebase debate is **honest history vs clean history**.

- **Merge** records what really happened (messy graph); safe on shared branches.
- **Rebase** gives a tidy linear story but rewrites hashes — unsafe once shared.
- **Local & unpushed** → rebase to clean up.
- **Already pushed / others have it** → merge, never force-push.
- **Golden rule:** rewrite only your own local history.

blocks.subTitle: Workflow choice
blocks.markdown:
Isolation vs integration frequency drives the workflow.

- **Trunk-based** — tiny short-lived branches, integrate many times a day behind feature flags. Minimal drift, needs strong CI.
- **PR flow** — short feature branch → pull request → review + CI → merge. The common middle ground.
- **GitFlow** — long-lived branches; heavy, fits scheduled releases with multiple maintained versions.

blocks.subTitle: Pull-request flow
blocks.markdown:
The dominant industry workflow is a social layer on plain Git branches.

![Pull-request branching workflow](assets/git-version-control/pr-workflow.svg)

- Branch off main → push → open a **pull request** → review + CI → merge.
- Merge buttons: merge commit, **squash**, or rebase-and-merge.
- The Linux kernel instead uses email patches + maintainer pulls — pure distributed Git, no central server of record.

blocks.subTitle: Recovery & undo
blocks.markdown:
Most Git emergencies are routine recoveries.

- **`git reflog`** records where HEAD has been — orphaned commits survive ~30–90 days, so a bad rebase is recoverable.
- **`revert`** makes a new commit undoing a change — safe for shared history.
- **`reset`** moves the branch pointer — local only. *Revert in public, reset in private.*
- **`--force-with-lease`** force-pushes safely, refusing if someone else pushed.

The misconceptions that bite:

- **"A branch is a copy of my files."** It's one pointer to a commit — switching just re-materializes a snapshot.
- **"Git stores diffs."** It stores full snapshots; diffs are computed on demand.
- **"`git add` adds the file."** It stages the *content at that moment* — later edits aren't staged.
- **"Rebase is a prettier merge."** It rewrites commits; destructive on shared branches.
- **"Deleting a secret in a later commit removes it."** History keeps it — purge and rotate.
